questions.prompt: A published application is deployed to App Service from a ZIP archive. What archive layout does the documented deployment process require?

options.text: Deployable application files at the ZIP root.
options.explanation: A surrounding parent folder can prevent the app from finding its expected files.

options.text: All application files nested inside an arbitrary extra parent directory.
options.explanation: The required root layout should not include an extra wrapping folder.

options.text: Only an empty folder named wwwroot.
options.explanation: An empty archive cannot supply the application.

options.text: Only the source repository URL stored in a text file.
options.explanation: ZIP package deployment needs the actual deployable application files.

questions.prompt: What happens when an administrator changes App Service app settings?

options.text: The settings are supplied as environment variables and the app restarts.
options.explanation: App Service applies configuration changes through its app settings mechanism.

options.text: The App Service plan changes operating system automatically.
options.explanation: Environment settings do not convert the plan OS.

options.text: A new staging slot is always created.
options.explanation: Changing app settings does not create a slot.

options.text: The application image is necessarily rebuilt and pushed to ACR.
options.explanation: Settings changes do not require a container build or image push.

questions.prompt: A web app has managed identity enabled but receives authorization failures from a protected Azure service. What should be checked?

options.text: The identity has the required role or access policy on that target service.
options.explanation: Authentication through managed identity still requires target-service authorization.

options.text: Assume enabling identity grants Contributor to every service.
options.explanation: Identity creation does not grant broad Azure access.

options.text: Change the web app display name to the service name.
options.explanation: Matching names do not grant authorization.

options.text: Increase plan workers as the only permission fix.
options.explanation: Additional workers do not change identity permissions.

questions.prompt: An App Service app has automatic backups and stores business data in an externally mounted Azure file share. What should the recovery design include?

options.text: Separate protection and restore procedures for the mounted share.
options.explanation: Automatic App Service backups exclude custom-mounted Azure storage.

options.text: Assume every mounted share is included in the automatic app backup.
options.explanation: The documented scope does not include that external storage.

options.text: Use an app-setting rename to bring the share into the backup.
options.explanation: Renaming configuration does not change the backup coverage.

options.text: Treat the source-code ZIP as a backup of all business data.
options.explanation: The deployment artifact does not contain independently stored application data.

questions.prompt: Before replacing a production App Service app with a backup, which approach provides useful recovery evidence?

options.text: Restore to a supported separate app or slot and test the app and dependencies.
options.explanation: A recovery test checks usable behavior and configuration beyond backup job status.

options.text: Only check that the backup list contains a timestamp.
options.explanation: A recorded backup does not prove the application can function after restoration.

options.text: Edit the backup ZIP manually to make its timestamp newer.
options.explanation: Altering backup artifacts can invalidate recovery.

options.text: Assume app restoration recreates every identity and network dependency.
options.explanation: Several related configurations and external services need separate recovery.

questions.prompt: In October 2026, you design a new App Service recovery setup with Azure SQL. Which database backup approach follows current Microsoft guidance?

options.text: Use Azure SQL native backup and restore alongside app protection.
options.explanation: Microsoft recommends native database tools, and new linked SQL backup configurations were removed in April 2026.

options.text: Depend on creating a new App Service linked SQL backup configuration.
options.explanation: The documented removal schedule has already removed this option for new configurations.

options.text: Assume automatic App Service backups include the SQL database.
options.explanation: Automatic backups do not include linked databases.

options.text: Use a deployment-slot swap as the only database backup.
options.explanation: A slot swap does not create a recoverable database backup.

questions.prompt: You map www.example.com to an App Service app and want DNS to follow its default hostname rather than a fixed IP. Which routing record does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: A CNAME from www to the app default hostname.
options.explanation: CNAME maps the subdomain to the hostname.

options.text: A TXT record containing only the app IP.
options.explanation: TXT verification is not traffic routing.

options.text: An MX record targeting the app hostname.
options.explanation: MX controls mail delivery, not web traffic resolution.

options.text: An NS record delegating www to the app hostname.
options.explanation: An app hostname is not an authoritative DNS nameserver.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the asuid.www TXT record when configuring www.example.com for App Service?

options.text: Prove domain ownership and help prevent another app claiming the hostname.
options.explanation: The domain verification ID supports ownership verification and takeover protection.

options.text: Route HTTPS packets to the app private IP.
options.explanation: TXT records do not route client traffic.

options.text: Store the certificate private key for browsers.
options.explanation: A public TXT record must not contain a private key.

options.text: Set the App Service plan worker count.
options.explanation: DNS verification does not configure compute capacity.

questions.prompt: www.example.com resolves to the correct App Service address, but the app has no custom-hostname entry for it and requests return a platform 404. What should be configured?

options.text: Validate and add the hostname binding to the intended app.
options.explanation: App Service must associate that Host header with the app.

options.text: Only lower the DNS TTL repeatedly.
options.explanation: Correct resolution cannot replace the missing app mapping.

options.text: Only add another identical A record.
options.explanation: Duplicating routing does not establish the hostname binding.

options.text: Only scale out the plan.
options.explanation: Additional workers do not register the custom hostname.

questions.prompt: An App Service app must call a VM using its private IP in a same-region VNet. Which App Service networking feature provides the outbound VNet path?

options.text: Regional VNet integration
options.explanation: It routes outbound calls from the app into the integrated network.

options.text: Only a private endpoint for the web app
options.explanation: That provides inbound private access to the app.

options.text: Only an app custom-domain binding
options.explanation: A hostname binding does not create the outbound VNet path.

options.text: Only an inbound IP access restriction
options.explanation: Inbound filtering does not configure private outbound routing.

questions.prompt: Users must access an App Service app privately from a VNet, and the app must also reach a private database. Which TWO capabilities should be configured for their respective traffic directions?

options.text: An App Service private endpoint for inbound requests
options.explanation: The endpoint exposes the app through a private IP.

options.text: VNet integration for the app outbound database connection
options.explanation: Integration provides outbound network access.

options.text: VNet integration alone as proof of private inbound access
options.explanation: Integration does not provide private inbound app access.

options.text: The app private endpoint alone as proof of private outbound database routing
options.explanation: The inbound endpoint does not configure outbound integration.

questions.prompt: A web app already uses a delegated subnet for VNet integration. Where should its inbound private endpoint be placed?

options.text: In a different suitable subnet.
options.explanation: The integration and private endpoint subnets must be different.

options.text: Always in the same delegated integration subnet.
options.explanation: App Service documents separate subnet requirements for these features.

options.text: In the app deployment slot instead of a subnet.
options.explanation: A slot is an application resource, not a network subnet.

options.text: In a DNS record with no private endpoint NIC.
options.explanation: DNS alone cannot create a private endpoint network interface.

questions.prompt: Two web apps and a staging slot run in the same dedicated App Service plan. What compute relationship should the administrator expect?

options.text: They share the plan worker capacity.
options.explanation: Apps and slots consume resources from the same dedicated plan.

options.text: Each receives an independently billed dedicated worker set automatically.
options.explanation: Dedicated compute is allocated at plan level.

options.text: The staging slot runs in a different region automatically.
options.explanation: A slot uses the same hosting plan, not automatic regional isolation.

options.text: Stopping one app deletes the shared plan workers.
options.explanation: App lifecycle operations do not delete the plan.

questions.prompt: A resource-intensive app must have an independent compute and scaling boundary from other apps. Which design fits?

options.text: Place it in a separate App Service plan.
options.explanation: A separate plan separates the worker capacity and plan scaling.

options.text: Create only another deployment slot in the existing plan.
options.explanation: Slots still share the existing plan workers.

options.text: Change only the app resource group while retaining the plan.
options.explanation: Resource-group organization does not separate shared compute.

options.text: Assign a different custom hostname while retaining the plan.
options.explanation: DNS naming does not change the compute boundary.

questions.prompt: The only app in a paid dedicated App Service plan is stopped. What should be checked to stop unnecessary plan compute charges?

options.text: Whether the unused plan can be deleted or moved to a suitable lower tier.
options.explanation: The plan retains its allocated paid capacity while the app is stopped.

options.text: Assume the stopped app makes the dedicated plan free.
options.explanation: Billing is based on allocated plan resources.

options.text: Remove only the app custom domain.
options.explanation: Hostname configuration does not release the plan compute.

options.text: Delete only the app deployment history.
options.explanation: Deployment records do not determine worker allocation.

questions.prompt: An App Service app needs more memory per worker and a higher-tier feature. Which operation addresses these requirements?

options.text: Scale up the App Service plan to a suitable SKU.
options.explanation: Scale up changes worker resources and tier features.

options.text: Only increase worker count with the existing SKU.
options.explanation: Scale out adds workers but does not increase memory per worker or unlock higher-tier features.

options.text: Only add a staging slot.
options.explanation: A slot consumes the existing plan capacity.

options.text: Only set a larger maximum autoscale count.
options.explanation: A count limit does not change the worker SKU.

questions.prompt: An App Service plan must run more instances at 08:00 each weekday based on a schedule. Which scaling mechanism should be used?

options.text: Azure Monitor autoscale with a scheduled profile.
options.explanation: Autoscale supports schedules for plan capacity.

options.text: App Service automatic scaling based only on HTTP traffic.
options.explanation: HTTP automatic scaling does not express the requested time-based schedule.

options.text: A deployment-slot swap at 08:00.
options.explanation: Swapping code slots does not define scheduled worker capacity.

options.text: A higher SKU without any scheduled scaling configuration.
options.explanation: Changing tier does not implement the requested daily instance schedule.

questions.prompt: You evaluate App Service automatic HTTP scaling. Which TWO points belong in the cost and compatibility review?

options.text: Prewarmed instances are billable.
options.explanation: Automatic scaling reserves a buffer whose instance time is charged.

options.text: Deployment-slot traffic is unsupported for this scaling feature.
options.explanation: The documented automatic scaling feature does not scale based on slot traffic.

options.text: It is the same configuration as Azure Monitor schedule rules.
options.explanation: Automatic HTTP scaling and Azure Monitor autoscale are distinct.

options.text: It provides paid Premium features on Free plans.
options.explanation: The feature requires supported Premium tiers.

questions.prompt: Production and staging use different database connection strings, and each must remain attached to its environment during a slot swap. What should be configured?

options.text: Mark the connection strings as deployment slot settings.
options.explanation: Sticky connection strings remain associated with their slot.

options.text: Leave them swappable and rely on different display names.
options.explanation: Display names do not prevent connection string swapping.

options.text: Put both connection strings only in the shared plan name.
options.explanation: The plan name does not supply environment-specific application configuration.

options.text: Change only the staging traffic percentage.
options.explanation: Traffic routing does not make connection strings sticky.

questions.prompt: Which App Service configuration remains with its slot during a swap?

options.text: Managed identity
options.explanation: Managed identities are listed among settings that do not swap.

options.text: All application content
options.explanation: Content is the main item moved between slots.

options.text: Every ordinary unmarked app setting
options.explanation: App settings can swap unless configured sticky or subject to documented exceptions.

options.text: All runtime framework settings
options.explanation: Framework settings are among the swappable configuration items.

questions.prompt: A release is swapped from staging to production and performs an external database schema migration. What does swapping the slots back provide?

options.text: A code/configuration rollback path that still needs a separate database compatibility or recovery plan.
options.explanation: A slot swap does not undo external database mutations.

options.text: Automatic reversal of every database change.
options.explanation: External data is outside the slot content swap.

options.text: Automatic restoration of all production data from Azure Backup.
options.explanation: Swap does not trigger database restoration.

options.text: Deletion of the newer database schema with guaranteed zero data loss.
options.explanation: A swap has no such schema or data-loss guarantee.

questions.prompt: A valid certificate for www.example.com has been uploaded to App Service, and the custom hostname is mapped, but HTTPS still does not use it. What configuration is missing?

options.text: A TLS binding associating the hostname with the certificate.
options.explanation: Upload stores the certificate; the binding selects it for the hostname.

options.text: Only another copy of the same certificate file.
options.explanation: Duplicate upload does not create the missing binding.

options.text: Only a larger App Service instance count.
options.explanation: Worker count does not associate a certificate with a hostname.

options.text: Only a DNS TTL of zero.
options.explanation: TTL does not configure the app TLS binding.

questions.prompt: An app requires a wildcard certificate covering *.example.com. Which certificate approach fits App Service requirements?

options.text: Import or upload a suitable wildcard certificate from a certificate provider.
options.explanation: A supported certificate with the required names can be bound to the app.

options.text: Request a free App Service managed wildcard certificate.
options.explanation: The free managed certificate does not support wildcards.

options.text: Use the default azurewebsites.net certificate for example.com.
options.explanation: The default certificate does not cover the custom domain.

options.text: Create only an ownership TXT record and omit TLS binding.
options.explanation: Domain ownership verification does not provide wildcard TLS.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an SNI TLS binding in App Service?

options.text: Select the certificate by hostname while sharing an IP address.
options.explanation: Server Name Indication communicates the requested hostname during TLS.

options.text: Require a separate dedicated IP for every hostname.
options.explanation: That is not the purpose of SNI.

options.text: Automatically create all external DNS records.
options.explanation: TLS binding does not administer the DNS provider.

options.text: Encrypt application data stored on the filesystem.
options.explanation: A TLS binding protects transport connections, not filesystem storage.

questions.prompt: Which Container Apps change creates a new revision?

options.text: Changing the container image in the app template
options.explanation: Container image configuration is revision-scoped.

options.text: Changing only an existing secret value
options.explanation: Secret values are application-scoped; revisions may need restarting to consume changes.

options.text: Changing only ingress traffic weights
options.explanation: Traffic configuration is application-scoped.

options.text: Adding only a managed identity
options.explanation: Changing the identity does not itself create a new revision.

questions.prompt: You want two Container Apps image versions active simultaneously, with 10% of ingress traffic sent to the new version. Which revision mode supports this?

options.text: Multiple revision mode
options.explanation: It supports concurrent active revisions and traffic splitting.

options.text: Single revision mode as the steady deployment state
options.explanation: Single mode does not keep multiple active application versions for this canary design.

options.text: An ACI restart policy of Always
options.explanation: ACI restart policies are a different service mechanism.

options.text: Disabling ingress for all revisions
options.explanation: That prevents the required incoming traffic split.

questions.prompt: A Container App image pulls successfully, but HTTP ingress cannot reach the process. The process listens on 8080 while ingress targets 80. What should be corrected?

options.text: Set the ingress target port to the actual listening port.
options.explanation: Ingress must forward to the port served by the container.

options.text: Grant the image publisher a broader push role only.
options.explanation: The image has already been pulled; publishing rights do not fix runtime routing.

options.text: Change only the revision label to 8080.
options.explanation: Labels do not set container listening or target ports.

options.text: Increase maximum replicas without changing the port.
options.explanation: More replicas with the same port mismatch remain unreachable.

questions.prompt: Two Linux containers in the same ACI container group need to communicate on an internal-only port. Which address can they use?

options.text: localhost with the listening port
options.explanation: Containers in a group share a local network.

options.text: Only a public load-balancer frontend
options.explanation: A public frontend is unnecessary for same-group communication.

options.text: Only a separate VNet peering for each container
options.explanation: Containers in one group do not each require a peered VNet.

options.text: The ACR repository URL as the runtime service address
options.explanation: A registry stores images; it is not the running service endpoint.

questions.prompt: An ACI batch task should retry after a nonzero process exit and remain terminated after successful completion. Which restart policy explicitly expresses that behavior?

options.text: OnFailure
options.explanation: This policy restarts failed processes but does not restart successful completion.

options.text: Always
options.explanation: Always also restarts the container after successful completion.

options.text: Never as a guarantee of exactly-once execution
options.explanation: Current documentation warns that nonzero exits can still be restarted; it is not an exactly-once guarantee.

options.text: An HTTP replica scaling rule
options.explanation: Replica scaling is not an ACI restart-policy value.

questions.prompt: Output from an ACI task must survive deletion of its container group. Which design meets the requirement?

options.text: Write results to durable external storage and retain that storage.
options.explanation: Data durability must extend beyond the container-group lifecycle.

options.text: Store the only copy in the container writable layer.
options.explanation: Deleting and recreating the group does not preserve that layer as a durable archive.

options.text: Use Always restart policy instead of persistent storage.
options.explanation: Restart policy does not provide durable output after deletion.

options.text: Give the group a DNS label and store output only locally.
options.explanation: A DNS label does not persist container filesystem contents.

questions.prompt: An ACR registry uses RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions. A workload must pull an image from an allowed repository but has only AcrPull. What should be changed?

options.text: Assign Container Registry Repository Reader with any condition covering the repository.
options.explanation: ABAC-enabled registries use the repository roles rather than legacy AcrPull.

options.text: Keep AcrPull and only refresh the token indefinitely.
options.explanation: A token refresh cannot make an unhonored role grant access.

options.text: Assign only Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister.
options.explanation: Listing repository names is not permission to pull their images.

options.text: Assign only Reader on the registry resource.
options.explanation: Control-plane read does not grant repository image access in ABAC mode.

questions.prompt: A deployment must refer to the exact same container image content after a tag is reassigned. Which identifier should it record?

options.text: The image digest
options.explanation: A digest identifies content rather than a mutable tag label.

options.text: Only the latest tag
options.explanation: latest is a mutable tag and may refer to different content later.

options.text: Only the repository name
options.explanation: A repository can contain many image versions.

options.text: Only the registry resource group
options.explanation: A management container does not identify image content.

questions.prompt: A supported Azure service must pull private ACR images without storing a shared registry password. Which approach fits?

options.text: Use its managed identity with the appropriate image pull role for the registry mode.
options.explanation: Managed identity authentication avoids a shared password and still requires authorization.

options.text: Enable the registry admin account and embed its password in the image.
options.explanation: This stores a shared secret and exposes it in the artifact.

options.text: Assign only a display name to the managed identity without roles.
options.explanation: An identity still requires permission to pull the repository.

options.text: Give the registry a public endpoint and assume images become anonymous.
options.explanation: Network reachability does not provide repository authorization.

questions.prompt: An ACI group has two containers requesting one CPU each. One container has a limit of two CPUs. What does that limit allow?

options.text: Use up to two CPUs when available within the allocated group resources.
options.explanation: A limit permits borrowing available allocation; it does not expand the group beyond its requested capacity.

options.text: Automatically create a second container-group replica.
options.explanation: Container resource limits do not create replicas.

options.text: Reserve four CPUs for the group automatically.
options.explanation: The requests total two CPUs, not four.

options.text: Guarantee two dedicated CPUs for each container simultaneously.
options.explanation: Both containers cannot each consume two CPUs from a two-CPU allocation.

questions.prompt: A Container Apps queue worker has ingress disabled, minReplicas 0, and no custom scale rule. Why can it remain at zero while queue messages arrive?

options.text: No configured trigger observes the queue and requests replicas.
options.explanation: Without ingress or a custom event rule, queue arrivals do not wake the app.

options.text: maxReplicas always forces at least that many replicas to run.
options.explanation: Maximum is a limit, not the requested minimum.

options.text: Changing the image tag in ACR automatically processes the queue.
options.explanation: An image tag does not configure an event scaler.

options.text: The inactive replica can measure its own CPU and wake itself.
options.explanation: There is no running replica producing that utilization signal.

questions.prompt: Every Container Apps replica fails during startup because its memory allocation is too small. Which change directly addresses that failure?

options.text: Choose a supported larger per-replica memory allocation and deploy the revision.
options.explanation: Each replica needs enough memory to start successfully.

options.text: Raise only maxReplicas while preserving the insufficient allocation.
options.explanation: More failing replicas do not increase memory available to each process.

options.text: Lower minReplicas to zero and leave the image unchanged.
options.explanation: A lower minimum does not fix the startup memory requirement.

options.text: Change only the ingress traffic percentage.
options.explanation: Traffic distribution does not enlarge the container memory allocation.

questions.prompt: An ARM template must accept only Standard_LRS or Standard_ZRS for a storageSku input. Which parameter property enforces this during validation?

options.text: allowedValues
options.explanation: The supplied value must be a member of this array.

options.text: defaultValue
options.explanation: A default supplies an omitted value; it does not restrict explicit input.

options.text: metadata.description
options.explanation: This documents the parameter without enforcing an allowed set.

options.text: minLength
options.explanation: Length validation cannot restrict the input to these two SKU names.

questions.prompt: An ARM incremental deployment redeclares an existing resource but omits one of its non-default properties. What should the administrator assume when reviewing the change?

options.text: The omitted property can reset to its default; declare the full intended configuration.
options.explanation: Incremental applies the resource definition rather than a partial property patch.

options.text: Every omitted property is preserved because the mode is incremental.
options.explanation: The preservation rule concerns omitted resources, not omitted properties on redeclared resources.

options.text: The entire resource is deleted because its definition changed.
options.explanation: Incremental does not delete the resource merely because a property is omitted.

options.text: Only the template contentVersion controls whether the property changes.
options.explanation: contentVersion is template metadata, not an update switch.

questions.prompt: An ARM template accepts an administrator password. Which TWO choices help prevent exposing it in template and deployment records?

options.text: Declare the input as secureString.
options.explanation: Secure parameters are not stored as plain values in deployment history.

options.text: Avoid hard-coded secrets and ordinary outputs containing the password.
options.explanation: A secure input can still be exposed by how the template author uses it.

options.text: Use a string parameter with a password-like name.
options.explanation: The name does not give a regular string secure handling.

options.text: Put the password in defaultValue in the public template.
options.explanation: Secure parameter handling does not hide a literal in the source file.

questions.prompt: You rename a Bicep symbolic identifier from store to archive, updating all code references but retaining the resource type, Azure name, scope, and properties. What does this change itself do?

options.text: Refactors the code without changing the Azure resource identity.
options.explanation: The deployed identity uses type, name, and scope, not the local symbol.

options.text: Renames the deployed account to archive.
options.explanation: The Azure name property was retained.

options.text: Deletes the resource formerly represented by store.
options.explanation: Changing only the symbol does not request deletion.

options.text: Moves the resource into a deployment named archive.
options.explanation: A symbolic identifier does not select deployment scope or history name.

questions.prompt: What does a successful az bicep build establish before an Azure deployment?

options.text: The file can compile to an ARM template.
options.explanation: Build performs compilation and reports Bicep diagnostics.

options.text: The deployment identity has all required Azure permissions.
options.explanation: Local compilation does not establish RBAC access.

options.text: The target region has capacity for every VM.
options.explanation: Allocation happens during deployment, not compilation.

options.text: All Azure Policy assignments permit the resources.
options.explanation: Policy evaluation depends on the Azure scope and resource request.

questions.prompt: A Bicep declaration uses existing for a virtual network in another resource group. Which TWO statements are correct?

options.text: The declaration references the virtual network without redeploying it.
options.explanation: existing describes an already deployed resource.

options.text: Its scope must identify the resource group containing that network.
options.explanation: The resource must be resolved at its actual scope.

options.text: The network is created automatically when missing.
options.explanation: An existing reference does not provision a missing resource.

options.text: The declaration grants the deploying identity network access rights.
options.explanation: Bicep references do not grant RBAC permissions.

questions.prompt: You must deploy a Bicep file into an existing resource group. Which command family targets that scope?

options.text: az deployment group create
options.explanation: The group deployment command targets a resource group.

options.text: az deployment sub create
options.explanation: This targets a subscription deployment, not the requested group scope.

options.text: az deployment mg create
options.explanation: This targets a management group.

options.text: az deployment tenant create
options.explanation: This targets the tenant scope.

questions.prompt: Which operation previews an ARM or Bicep deployment without applying the proposed resource changes?

options.text: what-if
options.explanation: What-if compares the intended deployment with current resources.

options.text: create with a new deployment name
options.explanation: A different history name does not prevent resource changes.

options.text: deleting the previous deployment record
options.explanation: History deletion does not preview a new deployment.

options.text: compiling the Bicep file only
options.explanation: Compilation produces JSON without comparing Azure resources.

questions.prompt: A deployment identity has Contributor on a resource group. Its template creates a VM and an Azure role assignment. The VM succeeds, but role assignment creation is denied. What additional permission should you investigate?

options.text: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write at the assignment scope
options.explanation: Contributor does not grant role assignment administration.

options.text: Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read only
options.explanation: VM read permission does not authorize role assignments.

options.text: Microsoft.Resources/deployments/read only
options.explanation: Reading deployment history cannot authorize the denied assignment.

options.text: Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action only
options.explanation: Starting a VM is unrelated to granting Azure resource access.

questions.prompt: An administrator changed a VM configuration manually after its original ARM deployment. Which export is intended to capture the current resource configuration?

options.text: Export from the resource group or resource
options.explanation: This generates a template based on the current resource state.

options.text: Export only the original deployment from history
options.explanation: That retrieves the original template, not later manual changes.

options.text: Compile the original Bicep source again
options.explanation: Compilation does not discover drift in Azure.

options.text: Download only the original parameter file
options.explanation: Original inputs do not include subsequent manual changes.

questions.prompt: You have exported an ARM JSON template and want editable Bicep source. Which command performs the conversion?

options.text: az bicep decompile --file current.json
options.explanation: Decompile converts ARM JSON into a Bicep starting point.

options.text: az bicep build --file current.json
options.explanation: Build compiles Bicep to ARM JSON; it is the opposite direction.

options.explanation: That distinction applies to Blob-level anonymous access when the account permits it. Disallowing anonymous access at the account also blocks individual-blob reads.

options.text: Existing blobs remain readable anonymously, but newly uploaded blobs require credentials.
options.explanation: The account setting is not limited to blobs created after the change. It prohibits anonymous reads of both existing and new blobs.

questions.prompt: An operator has the management-plane Reader role on a storage account but no blob data role. A container creation request using Azure CLI with --auth-mode login fails with an authorization error. Network access is working. Which additional listed built-in role is the least privileged that supports container creation through the Blob service?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Contributor at the storage account scope
options.explanation: This role includes the container-write operation required by Create Container. Account scope covers creation of the new container.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader at the storage account scope

options.text: Reader at the subscription scope
options.explanation: Broadening management-plane read access does not grant the required container-write operation.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Owner at the storage account scope
options.explanation: It can support the task, but grants more privilege than the listed Data Contributor role; the question requires least privilege among these choices.

questions.prompt: An account permits anonymous access, but a newly created container retains its Private access level. What must an anonymous client expect when requesting a blob from that container?

options.text: Access is denied because the container still requires authorization.
options.explanation: Permitting anonymous access at the account does not automatically enable it for a private container.

options.text: The blob can be read because every container inherits anonymous access.
options.explanation: The account setting permits public container configuration; it does not make every container public.

options.text: The client can list blobs but cannot read their contents.
options.explanation: Private access does not grant anonymous listing rights.

options.text: Only blobs uploaded after the account setting changed are public.
options.explanation: Anonymous access is governed by account and container settings, not blob upload time.

questions.prompt: You are signed in to Azure CLI and have the required blob data role. You want a container command to explicitly use your Entra identity rather than attempt account-key authorization. Which argument selects that behavior?

options.explanation: Login mode explicitly selects the signed-in identity for data authorization.

options.text: --auth-mode key

options.text: --public-access off

options.text: --account-name <account>

questions.prompt: A user has no existing Azure roles. They must navigate to a storage account in the Azure portal and read blobs in its reports container using Entra credentials. Network access is allowed. Which two role assignments meet that goal without granting resource-management writes or blob-data writes?

options.text: Reader at the storage account scope
options.explanation: Reader provides storage-account management visibility for portal navigation, without management writes. It supplies no blob-data read permission by itself.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader at the reports container scope
options.explanation: This provides Entra read access to the required container's blobs without blob-data writes. Together with account Reader, it meets both data access and portal navigation requirements.

options.text: Storage Queue Data Reader at the storage account scope
options.explanation: This grants queue access, not read access to reports blobs. Pairing it with management Reader leaves the blob-data requirement unsatisfied.

options.text: Contributor at the storage account scope

questions.prompt: A standard general-purpose v2 account stores block blobs that are rarely read but must remain immediately readable. Each blob will be deleted 45 days after upload. Which listed tier has lower capacity costs than hot and allows that deletion without an early-deletion charge?

options.text: Cool
options.explanation: Cool remains online, has lower capacity costs than hot, and has a 30-day minimum billed duration. Deletion after 45 days meets all three requirements.

options.text: Archive
options.explanation: Archive is offline and requires rehydration before content reads. It also has a 180-day minimum billed duration, so deletion after 45 days would incur an early-deletion charge.

options.text: Cold
options.explanation: Cold supports immediate reads and lower capacity costs, but its 90-day minimum billed duration exceeds the specified 45 days. Early deletion would incur a charge.

options.text: Hot
options.explanation: Hot provides immediate reads without a minimum billed duration. However, the requirement explicitly asks for lower capacity costs than hot; hot itself does not meet that comparison.

questions.prompt: A block blob is uploaded directly to cool in a general-purpose v2 account and deleted exactly 12 days later. Soft delete is disabled and no retention protection applies. How many additional days of cool storage does the early-deletion charge cover?

options.text: 18 days
options.explanation: Cool has a 30-day minimum billed duration in this account type. The blob was stored for 12 days, so the additional charge covers 30 minus 12, or 18 days.

options.text: 30 days
options.explanation: Thirty days is the total minimum billed duration, not an additional 30 days on top of the 12 already stored. The remaining duration is 18 days.

options.text: 0 days
options.explanation: Deletion is permitted, but it does not waive the minimum-duration charge. Removing the blob after 12 days leaves 18 billable days.

options.text: 12 days
options.explanation: Twelve days is the elapsed storage period. The early-deletion charge covers the unfulfilled portion of the 30-day minimum, which is 18 days.

questions.prompt: Blob A inherits its account's hot default tier. Blob B is explicitly set to hot. The account default is changed to cool. Which blob follows the new default without a separate blob-level tier operation?

options.text: Blob A only
options.explanation: An inferred tier follows the account default; an explicitly assigned tier does not.

options.text: Blob B only
options.explanation: This reverses the distinction between inferred and explicitly assigned tiers.

options.text: Both blobs
options.explanation: An account default change does not overwrite Blob B's explicit tier assignment.

options.text: Neither blob; defaults only affect future uploads
options.explanation: The default also applies to existing blobs whose tier is inferred.

questions.prompt: A Set Blob Tier request to archive fails for a block blob in a standard general-purpose v2 account using ZRS. The blob has no encryption scope. The request explicitly sets the individual blob tier; network access and data permissions are valid. Which configuration explains the failure?

options.text: The account uses a redundancy configuration that does not support archive.
options.explanation: Archive supports LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS, but not ZRS. The account redundancy therefore prevents this explicit blob-level transition.

options.text: The account is a premium block blob account that does not support standard access tiers.
options.explanation: Premium block blob accounts have this tiering limitation, but the stated account is standard general-purpose v2. That otherwise valid limitation does not explain this failure.

options.text: The object is an append blob, which does not support access-tier changes.
options.explanation: Access-tier changes apply to block blobs rather than append blobs. This object is explicitly a block blob, so the blob-type restriction does not explain the failure.

options.text: The request attempts to make archive the account default tier.
options.explanation: Archive cannot be an account default, but this request explicitly changes an individual blob. The unsupported account-default setting is not being requested.

questions.prompt: A team will migrate block blobs to a standard general-purpose v2 account. The known workload is suitable for cool and will retain the blobs for at least 60 days. Which two independent recommendations help the team control total tier-related costs?

options.text: Estimate read frequency and retrieval charges together with capacity and operation charges.
options.explanation: Microsoft recommends comparing total costs using the expected read pattern. Cool has lower capacity costs than hot but higher access costs, so capacity price alone is insufficient.

options.text: Upload the blobs directly to cool rather than first uploading to hot and immediately changing tiers.
options.explanation: When the appropriate tier is known, direct upload avoids the additional tier-change operation and the initial-tier capacity interval described in Microsoft guidance.

options.text: Use the cool capacity price as the complete cost estimate because the minimum duration will be met.
options.explanation: Meeting the minimum duration avoids an early-deletion charge for that retention plan. It does not remove cool retrieval or operation charges, which still belong in the estimate.

options.text: Upload to hot and immediately move to cool to avoid paying for a cool-tier write.
options.explanation: Moving to a cooler tier is billed as a write to the destination tier. Uploading first to hot adds the initial write rather than eliminating the later cool-tier operation.

questions.prompt: A lifecycle rule must target block blobs whose names begin with reports/ inside the study-records container. Which prefixMatch value targets that path?

options.text: study-records/reports/
options.explanation: A prefix begins with the container name, followed by the relevant blob-name prefix.

options.text: reports/
options.explanation: The required container name is missing; this does not target reports/ within study-records.

options.text: */reports/
options.explanation: Lifecycle prefixes do not use wildcard matching; the asterisk would be literal.

options.text: study-records/
options.explanation: This would include the entire container, rather than limiting the action to reports/.

questions.prompt: An enabled Blob lifecycle rule in a standard storage account uses prefixMatch invoices/2026/*.csv. The container is invoices, and a matching-type blob is named 2026/march.csv. Its age exceeds the configured threshold, but the rule does not select it. Which filter behavior explains this?

options.text: The filter interprets * as a literal character in the prefix.
options.explanation: The blob name does not contain a literal asterisk after 2026/. To select all names under that path, use invoices/2026/; that broader prefix would not restrict matches to CSV files.

options.text: The filter expects the account name before the container name.
options.explanation: A prefix starts with the container name. invoices is already the correct container component; adding the account name would target a different prefix.

options.text: The filter expects a complete HTTPS URL rather than a relative prefix.
options.explanation: prefixMatch accepts container/blob-name prefixes, not endpoint URLs. The problem is wildcard interpretation, not the absence of a hostname.

options.text: The filter compares the file extension instead of the beginning of the name.
options.explanation: The filter matches the beginning of the container/blob path. It does not interpret *.csv as an extension selector.

questions.prompt: A standard Blob Storage account contains a block blob explicitly assigned to the archive tier. You need to bring that existing blob into the hot tier. Which action starts rehydration?

options.text: Request Set Blob Tier with hot as the target tier.
options.explanation: An explicit tier change to an online tier starts archive rehydration. The blob is not readable immediately; rehydration must finish.

options.text: Set the storage account's default access tier to hot.
options.explanation: An account default applies to blobs with an inferred tier. It does not change this blob's explicitly assigned archive tier or initiate rehydration.

options.text: Enable lifecycle auto-tier-to-hot when the blob is accessed.
options.explanation: The lifecycle automatic promotion feature moves qualifying cool blobs to hot. It does not rehydrate archived blobs.

options.text: Issue a Get Blob request for the archived blob.
options.explanation: Archived content cannot be read until it is rehydrated into an online tier. A read request does not initiate that tier change.

questions.prompt: An enabled Blob lifecycle rule transitions current block blobs to cool when daysAfterModificationGreaterThan is 45. A matching blob was last modified 60 days ago, was read yesterday, and entered its current tier five days ago. No other age condition applies, and the tier transition is supported. Which assessment of its eligibility is correct?

options.text: It is eligible because its modification age exceeds 45 days.
options.explanation: The rule uses last modification: 60 is greater than 45. A read does not reset that timestamp. Eligibility permits a lifecycle action during processing; it does not prove the tier has already changed.

options.text: It is ineligible because its last read was fewer than 45 days ago.
options.explanation: That reasoning would evaluate a last-access-time condition. This rule instead evaluates the blob's last-modified timestamp.

options.text: It is ineligible because its current-tier age is fewer than 45 days.
options.explanation: The scenario has no last-tier-change condition. Five days in the current tier does not replace the configured 60-day modification age.

options.text: It is ineligible because its modification age must equal 45 days.
options.explanation: GreaterThan requires an age beyond the threshold, rather than equality. Sixty days satisfies the configured comparison.

questions.prompt: A storage account has three enabled lifecycle rules that must keep running. You are using Azure CLI to add a fourth rule through the account's management-policy API. The new rule has a distinct name. Which submitted policy preserves the existing rules and adds the new behavior?

options.text: A complete policy with all three existing rules and the new rule enabled.
options.explanation: The service writes the full policy. Including the retained enabled rules and the distinct new rule preserves the required configuration.

options.text: A policy containing only the new enabled rule, relying on rule-name merging.
options.explanation: The API does not merge a partial rule list into the saved policy. Omitting the existing rules would not preserve them.

options.text: A policy containing the most recent existing rule and the new rule enabled.
options.explanation: Submitting this smaller rule collection would omit two required rules. Their earlier existence does not preserve them through a full-policy replacement.

options.text: A complete policy with the three existing rules disabled and the new rule enabled.
options.explanation: The rules remain in the JSON but no longer process blobs. Retaining disabled definitions does not preserve the required existing behavior.

questions.prompt: You saved an enabled Blob lifecycle rule to transition eligible current block blobs from hot to cool ten minutes ago. The policy was accepted, but inspected blobs still have their original tier. Which two statements are correct when assessing this observation?

options.text: A policy change can take up to 24 hours to take effect and start execution.
options.explanation: The delay applies to activation and the start of the first run. Ten minutes without a tier change does not establish that the accepted rule is defective.

options.text: The rule's filters and age conditions determine which blobs can be processed.
options.explanation: An accepted policy still requires each object to match its filters and conditions. Check the saved definition against the inspected blobs before concluding that they should transition.

options.text: The 24-hour window guarantees completion for every eligible blob.
options.explanation: Microsoft describes when changes can take effect and a run can start, not a deadline for completing every object. Run duration depends on account workload and the number of blobs.

options.text: A read of an eligible hot blob triggers this tier-to-cool action immediately.
options.explanation: Lifecycle policy runs evaluate the tier-to-cool rule asynchronously. A read is not a synchronous trigger for this action; cool-to-hot access promotion is a different feature.

questions.prompt: In a flat-namespace Blob Storage account with versioning disabled, a blob is deleted while blob soft-delete retention is 7 days. Two days later, an administrator changes retention to 30 days. Which interval applies to that already-deleted blob?

options.text: The original 7-day interval, measured from deletion
options.explanation: The new retention setting applies to later deletions; it does not extend retention for this existing soft-deleted blob.

options.text: 30 days, measured from the original deletion
options.explanation: Increasing retention does not retroactively apply the new interval to previously deleted blobs.

options.text: 30 days, measured from the settings change
options.explanation: Changing account settings does not restart the retained blob's clock.

options.text: 7 days, measured from the settings change
options.explanation: Keeping the original duration does not restart its clock. The seven-day window remains measured from the original deletion, not from the change two days later.

questions.prompt: A flat-namespace storage account has blob and container soft delete disabled. Versioning is disabled and must remain disabled. A team must permit normal deletions, then recover either an individually deleted blob or a deleted container within seven days. Which two Blob service property changes are jointly required before those deletions occur?

options.text: Enable deleteRetentionPolicy with days set to 7.
options.explanation: This enables blob soft delete for individual blob recovery within seven days. Container protection alone cannot restore a blob deleted while its parent container remains.

options.text: Enable containerDeleteRetentionPolicy with days set to 7.
options.explanation: This enables recovery of a deleted container and its contents within seven days. Blob soft delete alone cannot recover a deleted parent container.

options.text: Enable isVersioningEnabled.
options.explanation: Versioning can preserve earlier blob states, but enabling it violates the explicit requirement to keep versioning disabled. It also does not provide recovery of a deleted container.

options.text: Set days to 7 on both retention policies while leaving enabled false.
options.explanation: A duration without an enabled policy does not activate soft-delete protection. Both policies must be enabled before the relevant deletion.

questions.prompt: An application overwrites a block blob using Put Blob in a flat-namespace account. Blob soft delete was enabled before the overwrite, versioning is disabled, and the retention window is still active. Undelete recovers the soft-deleted snapshot, but the current blob still contains the unwanted data. What additional action restores the earlier contents as current?

options.text: Copy the desired recovered snapshot over the current blob.
options.explanation: Undelete makes the snapshot available. Copying that snapshot over the original base blob promotes its earlier contents to the current contents, meeting the stated goal.

options.text: Run Restore Container for the parent container.
options.explanation: Restore Container recovers a deleted container. This parent still exists, and container recovery does not promote the already recovered snapshot over the current blob.

options.text: Run Undelete again on the current blob.
options.explanation: Undelete restores soft-deleted snapshots, which has already succeeded here. Repeating it does not overwrite the active blob with the chosen snapshot.

options.text: Copy the desired recovered snapshot to a new blob name.
options.explanation: This can make the earlier contents available as a separate blob. It leaves the original current blob unchanged, so it does not restore the earlier contents as current at the original blob.

questions.prompt: A Blob Storage account has retained soft-deleted blobs that have not expired. An administrator disables blob soft delete to change future protection behavior. What happens to those already-retained blobs?

options.text: They remain recoverable until their existing retention windows expire
options.explanation: Disabling the feature does not immediately purge data already retained under its original retention settings.

options.text: They are immediately permanently deleted
options.explanation: The configuration change does not override the existing retained objects' expiry times.

options.text: They are automatically restored to the active namespace
options.explanation: Disabling protection is not an Undelete operation.

options.text: Their expiry clocks pause until blob soft delete is enabled again
options.explanation: Disabling the setting does not suspend existing retention windows. The already-retained blobs remain recoverable only until their original windows expire.

questions.prompt: A container named invoices was soft-deleted yesterday. Its retention period has not expired, but another process created a new active invoices container. Blob soft delete is disabled. An attempt to restore the old container fails. Which stated condition explains the failure?

options.text: Container restoration requires the original name, which is already in use
options.explanation: The active replacement creates a name collision. Its data must be assessed before deciding how to free that name safely.

options.text: Containers cannot be restored until the final day of retention
options.explanation: Restoration is available during retention, not only at its end.

options.text: Blob soft delete is disabled, so container restoration is unavailable
options.explanation: Container soft delete can restore the deleted container and its contents without blob soft delete. The account has retained this container; the active same-name replacement is the blocking condition.

options.text: The old container must be restored under an arbitrary new name
options.explanation: This operation does not support restoring the old container under a different name.

questions.prompt: An Azure storage account had container soft delete enabled, but no blob soft delete, versioning, snapshots, or backup. A user deletes one blob while leaving its container intact. Which recovery outcome applies to the deleted blob?

options.text: Container soft delete cannot recover this individual deletion.
options.explanation: The parent container was not deleted, so there is no retained container state to restore. The blob needed applicable individual protection before deletion.

options.text: Restoring the active container rolls it back to its state before the blob deletion.
options.explanation: Container soft delete retains a container when the container is deleted. It does not record earlier states of an active container for point-in-time rollback.

options.text: Deleting and restoring the parent now recovers its state from before the blob deletion.
options.explanation: A later container deletion retains the state at that later deletion, when this blob is already missing. It cannot reconstruct the earlier unprotected blob.

options.text: Enabling blob soft delete now makes the earlier deletion recoverable.
options.explanation: Blob soft delete must protect the object when it is deleted. Enabling protection afterward does not create a retained copy of data already deleted without protection.

questions.prompt: You must verify that a storage account retains deleted containers. Its Blob service properties show deleteRetentionPolicy.enabled as true. Which additional property specifically verifies container protection?

options.text: containerDeleteRetentionPolicy.enabled
options.explanation: This flag activates retention for deleted containers. The stated deleteRetentionPolicy.enabled flag instead enables individual blob protection.

options.text: isVersioningEnabled
options.explanation: This saves earlier blob states; it does not activate retention of deleted parent containers. Versioning alone does not verify container protection.

options.text: deleteRetentionPolicy.days
options.explanation: This is the duration for the blob-level policy, not the activation flag for container retention. Its value does not establish that container protection is enabled.

options.text: restorePolicy.enabled
options.explanation: This enables point-in-time restoration of block blobs, a different recovery feature. It does not establish that whole-container deletion is retained for recovery.

questions.prompt: A design enables container soft delete and claims this alone will recover every container if the entire storage account is accidentally deleted. Which statement correctly identifies the gap?

options.text: Container soft delete does not protect deletion of the storage account itself
options.explanation: The recovery feature operates within an existing account. Account deletion needs separate controls, such as a resource lock, and an appropriate broader recovery design.

options.text: The design works whenever container retention is at least 30 days
options.explanation: A longer retention period does not expand the feature to account deletion.

options.text: Enabling blob versioning guarantees restoration of the deleted account
options.explanation: Blob versions are also held within the account and do not provide account restoration.

options.text: Containers already soft-deleted are protected from account deletion, but active containers are not
options.explanation: Retained containers are still inside the storage account. Their deleted status does not make container soft delete an account-deletion recovery feature; the boundary applies to active and retained container data alike.

questions.prompt: Blob versioning is enabled in a supported flat-namespace account. A client deletes a block blob without supplying a version ID. What is the immediate versioning result?

options.text: The current version becomes a previous version, and no current version remains
options.explanation: The delete operation preserves prior versions while removing the current-version position.

options.text: Every version is deleted permanently
options.explanation: Deleting without a version ID does not delete every previous version.

options.text: The oldest version automatically becomes current
options.explanation: Azure does not choose an older version to promote automatically.

options.text: The delete is always blocked while any previous version exists
options.explanation: Versioning allows this delete operation; it changes the current version into a previous one.

questions.prompt: An attempt to enable blob versioning fails on a standard general-purpose v2 account with hierarchical namespace enabled. The administrator has valid management permissions and uses an API version later than 2019-10-10. Blob soft delete is also enabled. Which stated configuration explains the failure?

options.text: Hierarchical namespace is enabled, which is unsupported for blob versioning.
options.explanation: Microsoft excludes accounts with hierarchical namespace from blob versioning support. The account satisfies the stated account-type and API prerequisites, but fails this namespace prerequisite.

options.text: Blob soft delete is enabled, which cannot coexist with blob versioning.
options.explanation: Microsoft recommends combining blob soft delete and versioning on supported accounts. Soft delete is not the incompatible feature; hierarchical namespace is.

options.text: The account is general-purpose v1, which lacks blob versioning support.
options.explanation: General-purpose v1 is outside the documented supported account types, but this account is explicitly general-purpose v2. That account-type limitation does not describe the scenario.

options.text: The request uses an API version older than 2019-10-10.
options.explanation: Blob versioning requires version 2019-10-10 or later. The request explicitly uses a later version, so the API prerequisite is met.

questions.prompt: A supported flat-namespace Blob Storage account has versioning and blob soft delete enabled. Reading the original blob without a version ID returns BlobNotFound: there is no current blob. The desired previous version was explicitly deleted but remains within soft-delete retention; the container still exists. Which two operations are jointly required, in the indicated order, to make that version's contents current at the original blob name?

options.text: First call Undelete Blob to restore the retained versions.
options.explanation: The desired version is soft-deleted, so it must be restored before its contents can be copied. Undelete restores the retained versions but does not create a current blob.

options.text: Then copy the desired previous version to the original base blob.
options.explanation: After Undelete makes the version available, Copy Blob creates a new current blob with those contents at the required original name.

options.text: Then copy the desired previous version to a different blob name.
options.explanation: This produces a separate blob after the version is restored. It does not make the version current at the required original blob name.

options.text: First restore the parent container using Restore Container.
options.explanation: The parent container still exists and was not deleted. Container restoration does not undelete the explicitly deleted blob versions in that existing container.

questions.prompt: A frequently overwritten block blob has accumulated many historical versions. The team wants to control retained storage and listing latency while keeping recent recovery points. Which approach follows Microsoft's version-management guidance?

options.text: Define lifecycle cleanup for previous versions using an appropriate retention requirement
options.explanation: A version-specific lifecycle policy can remove older versions while retaining the recovery history the workload needs.

options.text: Rely on automatic deletion as soon as the blob reaches 1,000 versions
options.explanation: Maintaining fewer than 1,000 versions is guidance, not an automatic oldest-version deletion rule.

options.text: Configure only a current-blob tiering rule and assume previous versions are deleted
options.explanation: A rule that only tiers the current blob does not define deletion of its previous versions.

options.text: Disable versioning to immediately purge all previous versions
options.explanation: Disabling new version creation does not delete versions that already exist.

questions.prompt: A classic SMB Azure file share has a snapshot from before an unwanted file overwrite. The live share still exists. How should an administrator recover the earlier file contents?

options.text: Read the file from the snapshot and restore or copy it to a writable destination
options.explanation: The snapshot provides an earlier read-only source. Recovery writes its contents to the live share or another destination.

options.text: Open the snapshot and edit its file contents in place
options.explanation: Share snapshots are read-only and cannot be edited in place.

options.text: Enable share soft delete to undo the existing file overwrite
options.explanation: Share soft delete protects whole-share deletion; it does not roll back an individual overwrite.

options.text: Create a new snapshot now and restore the file from that new snapshot
options.explanation: A new snapshot captures the current unwanted contents. The earlier snapshot is the required source for recovering the file state before the overwrite.

questions.prompt: On a classic SMB Azure file share, snapshot S1 captured report.csv at 09:00. After a file edit, S2 captured it at 10:00. The live file was deleted at 11:00. An administrator then deletes S1 but retains S2. What can be recovered from S2?

options.text: The report.csv contents captured at 10:00, despite deletion of S1 and the live file.
options.explanation: Each retained snapshot contains the information needed for its own point-in-time recovery. Deleting S1 removes only data unique to S1; S2 still preserves its captured file state.

options.text: Nothing from report.csv, because removing S1 breaks the incremental snapshot chain.
options.explanation: Azure Files manages shared snapshot data. Its incremental storage does not require the administrator to retain every earlier snapshot for S2 to remain usable.

options.text: Nothing from report.csv, because recovery requires the file to still exist in the live share.
options.explanation: A snapshot retains its captured state independently of later individual-file deletion. The live share exists, so the deleted file can be recovered from S2.

options.text: The report.csv contents captured at 09:00, because S2 takes over the deleted snapshot's state.
options.explanation: Deleting S1 does not change the time represented by S2. S2 remains the 10:00 recovery point and does not become the deleted 09:00 snapshot.

questions.prompt: A classic Azure file share has snapshots, but share soft delete and backup are disabled. An administrator proposes deleting the share and all its snapshots to free capacity, while relying on those snapshots for later recovery. What is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Those snapshots cannot be retained independently after the share and its snapshots are deleted
options.explanation: Snapshots belong to the share. With no separate recovery protection in the scenario, deleting them does not leave an independent backup.

options.text: Nothing; snapshots without an expiry setting persist even after explicit share deletion
options.explanation: Snapshots persist until explicitly deleted or until the share is deleted. Lack of a scheduled expiry does not preserve them after the requested share-and-snapshot deletion.

options.text: Nothing; read-only snapshots cannot be removed by an explicit delete operation
options.explanation: Read-only prevents modifying snapshot contents. It does not prevent deleting snapshots; the proposed operation removes the data needed for recovery.

options.text: Only the share name matters; recreating the name restores all snapshots
options.explanation: Reusing the deleted share's name cannot reconstruct removed snapshot data.

questions.prompt: An application deployment will change files on a classic SMB Azure file share. Before deployment, the administrator must establish a pre-deployment recovery point and confirm that the recovery operator can read its captured files and write the restoration destination. Which two actions jointly meet these readiness requirements?

options.text: Create a share snapshot before the application changes the files
options.explanation: The snapshot must capture the desired earlier state before the unwanted change occurs.

options.text: Verify the captured files and the permissions needed to copy them to a recovery destination
options.explanation: A recovery point is useful only if the operator can locate and read the intended contents and write the restoration destination.

options.text: Wait until after corruption is discovered to create the first snapshot of the earlier state
options.explanation: A new snapshot captures the state at creation; it cannot reconstruct previously overwritten contents.

options.text: Enable only share soft delete instead of preserving earlier file contents
options.explanation: Whole-share deletion protection does not supply the pre-overwrite file state required by this scenario.

questions.prompt: Share soft delete is enabled for a classic SMB Azure file share. A user deletes one file, but the share remains Active and has no deleted-share entry to undelete. A snapshot containing the file was taken earlier. Which recovery source applies?

options.text: The earlier share snapshot containing the file
options.explanation: A snapshot can provide earlier file contents. Share soft delete applies to deletion of the whole share.

options.text: Undelete the still-active share to reverse the individual file deletion
options.explanation: There is no deleted share to restore, and this operation does not roll an active share back.

options.text: Create a new share snapshot after the deletion and recover the file from it
options.explanation: A new snapshot captures the current state, in which the file is missing. It does not reconstruct the earlier file contents; the existing pre-deletion snapshot is the applicable source.

options.text: Use the file's automatically created Azure Blob version
options.explanation: Azure Files data does not automatically receive Blob Storage version IDs.

questions.prompt: You want a 14-day soft-delete window for classic Azure file shares in a storage account. Which configuration operation targets that protection?

options.text: Enable delete retention for 14 days in the account's File service properties.
options.explanation: Classic file-share soft delete is enabled through File service properties and applies across the shares in that account. This configures the requested 14-day recovery window.

options.text: Enable blob delete retention for 14 days in the account's Blob service properties.
options.explanation: Blob delete retention protects Blob Storage objects, not Azure file shares. The correct duration on the wrong service does not activate the required protection.

options.text: Enable container delete retention for 14 days in the account's Blob service properties.
options.explanation: Container delete retention protects Blob containers. A classic Azure file share belongs to the File service and requires its own share protection.

options.text: Set File service delete retention to 14 days while leaving its enabled flag false.
options.explanation: A configured duration does not enable protection when the policy remains disabled. The requested recovery window requires both activation and the 14-day duration.

questions.prompt: A classic Azure file share was deleted while share soft delete was enabled. Its retention window remains active, and the retained share contains files and snapshots. What does undeleting that share restore?

options.text: The share and its retained contents, including snapshots
options.explanation: Recovery returns the share and contents retained from its state before deletion, rather than creating an empty replacement.

options.text: Only an empty share with the original name
options.explanation: Soft-delete recovery includes the retained contents, not merely the namespace.

options.text: The files, but never the snapshots
options.explanation: Snapshots are included in the retained share's recovery.

options.text: The share and its snapshots, but not the retained live files
options.explanation: Undelete restores the retained share contents from before deletion, including both its files and snapshots. It does not restore only the historical snapshots while omitting the retained live files.

questions.prompt: You will restore a retained classic Azure file share using az storage share-rm restore. You know the account, resource group, and original share name. What additional value should you obtain from listing deleted shares?

options.text: The deleted share version returned for the retained share instance.
options.explanation: The --deleted-version argument identifies which retained deleted share instance to restore. The account, resource group, and name identify the resource context but do not replace that deletion version.

options.text: The Azure resource ID of the original file share.
options.explanation: A resource ID identifies a management resource, not the particular deleted share version required by --deleted-version. The restore operation separately requires the retained instance's version value.

options.text: The original file-share name.
options.explanation: The name is supplied through --name and is already known in the scenario. It does not replace the separate --deleted-version value returned by listing deleted shares.

options.text: A snapshot timestamp belonging to that same share.
options.explanation: A share snapshot identifies a file-share point-in-time source. It is a different identifier from the deleted-share version used by the whole-share restore command.

questions.prompt: A storage account allows anonymous blob access, and an ordinary container's anonymous access level is Blob. Networking permits the requests. Which operation is available to an anonymous client?

options.text: Read a known blob URL, but not list the container's blobs.
options.explanation: Blob-level anonymous access permits reads of individual blobs without anonymous container listing.

options.text: List all blobs and read their contents.
options.explanation: Anonymous listing requires Container-level access, not Blob-level access.

options.text: Upload blobs without a credential.
options.explanation: Anonymous access levels grant reads, not unauthenticated writes.

options.text: No blob reads because anonymous access always requires a SAS.
options.explanation: Under the stated account/container settings, anonymous individual-blob reads do not require a SAS.

questions.prompt: An approved legacy Azure CLI container operation must use a supplied account key. Shared Key access is enabled; no storage credential environment variables are set. The signed-in identity has a blob data role but cannot list the account's keys. Which authorization configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: --auth-mode login, with the signed-in identity's blob data role
options.explanation: Login authorizes the operation with the Entra identity. It does not use the supplied account key, even though the identity has data access.

options.text: --auth-mode key --account-key <supplied-account-key>

options.text: --auth-mode key, with no account key or SAS supplied
options.explanation: With no supplied credential or environment value, key mode attempts to obtain an account key. This identity lacks listKeys permission, so it cannot obtain the required credential.

options.text: --auth-mode key --sas-token <supplied-sas-token>
options.explanation: This supplies a SAS for authorization. A SAS is a different credential from the account key explicitly required by the legacy operation.

questions.prompt: All known consumers of an Azure storage account currently use key1. You need to rotate both keys while maintaining service. What should happen before regenerating key1?

options.text: Move all consumers to valid key2 and verify requests.
options.explanation: Move every known key1 consumer to valid key2 and verify data requests before regenerating key1. This preserves a working credential while the old key1 value and its signed SAS become invalid.

options.text: Regenerate both keys at the same time.

options.text: Enable a key rotation reminder while consumers continue using key1.
options.explanation: A rotation reminder prompts administrators; it does not update consumer connection strings or preserve the old key after regeneration. Consumers would still use invalid key1 once it is rotated.

options.text: Generate a long-lived SAS signed with the old key1.
options.explanation: That SAS also depends on the key being regenerated.

questions.prompt: Shared Key access is disabled on an Azure storage account. Which credential can still authorize a Blob read when its permissions, lifetime, and network path are valid?

options.text: A user delegation SAS.
options.explanation: Its signing authority is Entra-backed rather than an account key.

options.text: A service SAS signed by key1.
options.explanation: Blob service SAS authorization relies on Shared Key.

options.text: An account SAS signed by key2.
options.explanation: Changing which account key signed it does not bypass the restriction.

options.text: A connection string containing key1.
options.explanation: Embedding the key in a connection string does not change authorization type.

questions.prompt: An operator must list and regenerate keys for one storage account. The additional role must not grant general storage-account configuration writes. Which listed built-in role should be assigned at that account scope?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader.

options.text: Storage Blob Delegator.

questions.prompt: An on-premises client outside Azure has a valid read-only Blob SAS. Downloads fail after the storage account's public endpoint is restricted to selected networks. options.text: Replace the SAS with the storage account key.
